title: Hidden Valley land use plan approved with changes
subtitle: Parks master plan, Arlington Boulevard rezoning, park tree and bench program, heritage permits, noise exemptions and licensing penalties
overview: Council approved the City's Hidden Valley land use plan, with two changes requested by the landowner. Two of the three areas in dispute were redesignated as low-rise residential and removed from the natural heritage mapping. The northern commercial request was not granted. The former Hidden Valley community plans were repealed. The vote was {{vote:m1}}.

Council also approved the Places and Spaces Parks Master Plan {{vote:m2}}, which sets near-, mid- and long-term priorities for parks. A revised Park Tree and Bench Dedication Program was approved {{vote:m14}}. Council approved an official plan and zoning change for 44 and 50 Arlington Boulevard {{vote:m16}}, moved licensing violations into the Administrative Monetary Penalty System {{vote:m12}}, and granted noise exemptions for downtown special events and the Greek Food Festival.

Council approved five heritage permits, including the demolition of additions at 60 Victoria Street North while the 1913 building is kept. Council also recognized the Chief Administrative Officer and the General Manager of Corporate Services for years of service. It heard updates from Communitech and the Waterloo Regional Health Network on its RedDAY fundraiser.

decisions.detail: Council approved the official plan and zoning amendments with changes that redesignate two disputed areas as low-rise residential, zone them RES-5 and remove them from the natural heritage map, and repeal the old Hidden Valley community plans.

decisions.item: Places and Spaces Parks Master Plan
decisions.detail: Council approved the Parks Master Plan and directed staff to carry out its near-, mid- and long-term implementation framework.

decisions.item: Park Tree and Bench Dedication Program
decisions.detail: Council approved the revised program for dedicating trees and benches in parks.
Council approved the official plan amendment and zoning by-law amendment for the Arlington Boulevard properties.
Council enacted a by-law moving enforcement and adjudication of licensing violations into the City's Administrative Monetary Penalty System.
Council approved demolition of three additions while retaining the 1913 building in full, subject to conservation, structural, risk and protection plans.
Council granted an exemption to the noise chapter of the Municipal Code for all downtown special events.
Council granted a noise exemption for the festival at 527 Bridgeport Road on June 7 and 8, 2025.

debate: Representatives of the Hidden Valley landowner opposed parts of the staff recommendation. They said an environmental overlay area had been agreed with staff to be removed. They also argued that their consultant's analysis showed two areas did not meet the woodland criteria, and that one area was already designated residential and had approvals for five lots.

Several councillors said the site visit helped them see room for judgment on two of the three areas. One councillor said that, given the housing supply crisis, staff should generally take the more protective stance and Council could weigh other factors. Another noted that a large share of Hidden Valley is already protected and that the area is an entry point to the city.

The Parks Master Plan drew support from a resident group. It asked Council to prioritize parkland on City-owned sites, to green alternative spaces such as laneways without substituting them for parks, and to maximize trees in multipurpose spaces. It disagreed with adjusting expectations of what a park is downtown.
Councillors praised the Parks Master Plan as realistic and costed. They praised the tree and bench program for lowering the cost of a tree dedication to $50 and giving residents a clear process.

During the Communitech update, councillors asked about economic uncertainty, the role of AI, and whether other levels of government were adding support. Communitech's CEO cited tariffs and geopolitical uncertainty and said Communitech would help local firms adopt AI.
